block.caption: An earthquake. What is happening to the buildings? What are people doing right now?

models.title: Story · The day Japan moved (2011 earthquake)

block.label: STORY · THE DAY JAPAN MOVED
block.html:
On March 11, 2011, a huge earthquake hit the coast of Japan. It was a magnitude 9.0 earthquake, the strongest ever recorded in Japan. The ground shook for about six minutes. In Tokyo, tall buildings were swaying from side to side, but most of them didn't fall, because Japan builds them to move with the ground.

Later, scientists discovered something incredible: the earthquake moved Japan's main island about 2.4 meters to the east. It even changed the way the Earth spins, and every day became 1.8 microseconds shorter. You can't feel it, but your day is a tiny bit shorter because of this earthquake!

Sadly, the earthquake also caused a giant tsunami.

block.caption: A tsunami. If you were on this beach, what would you do?

models.title: Story · The girl who saved a beach (Tilly Smith, 2004)

block.label: STORY · THE GIRL WHO SAVED A BEACH
block.html:
In December 2004, Tilly Smith, a 10-year-old British girl, was on holiday with her family at Mai Khao Beach, in Thailand. While she was walking on the beach with her mother, she noticed something strange: the sea was bubbling, like the foam on a glass of beer, and it didn't look normal.

Two weeks before, her geography teacher, Mr. Kearney, taught the class about tsunamis and their warning signs. Tilly remembered the lesson and warned her parents that a tsunami was coming. At first, they weren't sure, but Tilly insisted. Her father told the hotel staff, and they evacuated the beach.

A few minutes later, giant waves hit the beach. Thanks to a geography lesson, about 100 people survived.

block.caption: A volcanic eruption. Why are the planes turning back? Look at the sign.

models.title: Story · The volcano nobody can pronounce (Iceland, 2010)

block.label: STORY · THE VOLCANO NOBODY CAN PRONOUNCE
block.html:
In April 2010, a volcano in Iceland called Eyjafjallajökull (say: AY-ya-fyat-la-YO-kutl) erupted. The eruption wasn't very big, but it sent a huge cloud of ash into the sky, and the wind carried the ash to Europe.

Ash is dangerous for airplane engines, so many countries closed their airspace. For about a week, almost no planes flew over northern Europe. More than 100,000 flights were cancelled, and about 10 million passengers were affected. Millions of travelers were stranded in airports around the world. Some people took trains, buses and even taxis across Europe to get home.

And on TV, news reporters were trying, and failing, to say the volcano's name!

block.caption: A landslide. What is sliding down the mountain? Where is it going?

models.title: Story · The man who refused to leave (Mount St. Helens, 1980)

block.label: STORY · THE MAN WHO REFUSED TO LEAVE
block.html:
In March 1980, Mount St. Helens, a volcano in the United States, woke up. Scientists warned everybody to leave the area. But one man refused: Harry R. Truman, 83 years old. He lived in a lodge next to Spirit Lake with his 16 cats, and he loved the mountain. He said that the mountain would never hurt him. He became famous, and hundreds of children wrote letters to him.

On the morning of May 18, an earthquake made the north side of the mountain collapse. It was the biggest landslide in recorded history: rocks and earth slid down at about 200 km/h, faster than a car on a highway. Then the volcano erupted. The landslide buried Spirit Lake and Harry's lodge. Harry was never found.

block.caption: A wildfire. What can animals do when a fire is coming? And people?

block.label: STORY · OUSADO, THE JAGUAR
block.html:
In 2020, huge wildfires spread across the Pantanal, in Brazil, the largest tropical wetland in the world. It was a very dry year, and the fires burned about 28% of the region. Many animals couldn't escape.

In September, volunteer vets found a male jaguar with terrible burns on all four paws. They called him Ousado (in English, daring). First, they took him to a veterinary hospital in Cuiabá, and then to a wild cat clinic in Goiás, where they treated his paws.

Ousado recovered well, and on October 20 the vets released him in the same place where they found him. He went back home with four healthy paws.

block.caption: A drought. Look at the reservoir: what was the water level before? And now?

block.label: STORY · DAY ZERO
block.html:
In 2018, Cape Town, a big city in South Africa, had a serious problem. After three years with very little rain, the city's dams were almost empty. The government announced Day Zero: the day when the city would turn off the water in people's homes. People would have to queue for water at special collection points.

To avoid Day Zero, everybody had to save water. Each person could use only 50 liters a day. A normal shower uses that in about 5 minutes! People took 2-minute showers, used old water to flush the toilet, and stopped watering their gardens. Nobody wanted to waste a single drop.

It worked: the city used about half the water it used before, the rain finally came back, and Day Zero never happened.

block.caption: A heatwave. Look at the train tracks and the thermometer. What happened?

models.title: Story · The day the runway melted (UK, 2022)

block.label: STORY · THE DAY THE RUNWAY MELTED
block.html:
On July 19, 2022, the United Kingdom reached 40°C for the first time in history. In Coningsby, a small town in England, the temperature was 40.3°C, a new national record.

The UK isn't ready for this kind of heat: most British homes don't have air conditioning. During the heatwave, roads melted, trains moved very slowly because the tracks were too hot, and a part of the runway at Luton Airport lifted because of the heat, so the airport stopped all flights for a few hours.

In Brazil, 40°C is a normal summer day in many cities. But for the British, it was unbearable.

block.caption: A blizzard. Look at the wires and the snow. How do people get to work?

models.title: Story · The Great White Hurricane (New York, 1888)

block.label: STORY · THE GREAT WHITE HURRICANE
block.html:
In March 1888, a terrible blizzard hit the east coast of the United States. People called it The Great White Hurricane. In New York, almost one meter of snow fell, and the strong wind made snowdrifts as tall as houses.

Everything stopped: trains, horses, even the mail. Many people were stuck at work or on trains, and some people crossed the frozen East River on foot! The wind also knocked down the electric and telephone wires that were above the streets.

After the blizzard, the city decided to put the wires underground, and the idea of an underground train became more popular. In 1904, New York opened its first subway line. Today, millions of New Yorkers use it every day.
